cues.text: Section ten: business continuity and resilience.
Let us begin with three related ideas that are easy to confuse.
Business continuity is about keeping critical business functions operating during a disruption.
Disaster recovery is narrower: it restores IT systems and data after a disruption.
Resilience is broader again.
It is the ability to withstand, adapt to and recover from adverse events.
To decide what matters most, an organisation carries out a business impact analysis, usually shortened to BIA.
A BIA identifies critical processes, their dependencies, and the consequences if they are interrupted.
From this, two key targets are set.
The recovery time objective, or RTO, is the target time within which service should be restored.
The recovery point objective, or RPO, is the maximum tolerable data loss, measured in time.
Consider an example.
If the RTO is two hours and the RPO is 15 minutes, the organisation aims to restore service within two hours and to lose no more than 15 minutes of data.
Notice what this implies for backups: daily backups alone cannot reliably meet that RPO, because a daily backup could leave far more than 15 minutes of data unprotected.
Next, recovery sites.
A hot site is highly prepared and typically supports rapid recovery, but at higher cost.
A warm site has prepared infrastructure, but needs additional restoration or configuration before it is ready.
A cold site provides only basic facilities and requires more setup.
Which one is appropriate depends on the business impact and the recovery objectives.
Now, backups.
Backups may be full, incremental or differential.
A full backup copies all the selected data.
An incremental backup copies the changes since the previous backup.
A differential backup copies the changes since the last full backup.
A useful guideline is the 3-2-1 principle: three copies of the data, on two media types, with one copy offsite.
Immutable or offline copies can improve resilience against ransomware.
And remember to test restoration, because a backup that cannot be restored is not a recovery capability.
Related to this are redundancy and failover.
Redundancy provides alternative components, and failover switches the service to a healthy component.
However, replication is not a substitute for backups, because corruption or deletion may be replicated too.
Likewise, high availability reduces downtime, but it does not replace disaster recovery.
Finally, continuity plans themselves.
A good plan specifies activation criteria, roles, communications, alternative processes, recovery priorities, exercises and review.
In Nigeria, unreliable power and connectivity make backup power, diverse network links and tested fallback processes particularly important.
